To choose between the imperfect (background, description, habit) and the compound perfect (event, finished action).
To tell about an interrupted action: "I was reading when the phone rang."
To organise a story: at first, then, after that, in the end.
To understand an oral story told in the past.
On Friday evening, Nora and Radu meet at Mr Grigore's café. It is raining outside. Nora asks Mr Grigore a question she has been thinking about for a week: why doesn't the big clock by the door work?
Mr Grigore, may I ask you something? I know the clock by the door belonged to Mr Vasile. What happened to it?
Ah… It's a long story. Wait, I'll bring you some tea. A long story deserves it, on an evening like this.
Grandpa never told me about the clock. I only know he loved it very much.

That pendulum clock is from 1890. It belonged to Vasile's grandfather. Back when we were young, Vasile kept it in the living room and wound it every Sunday. He used to say that a house without a ticking clock is a house without a heart.
And how did it end up here?

Ten years ago, Vasile fell ill. He was in hospital, weak and tired. One day, while I was visiting him, he told me: "Grigore, you take the clock. Elisabeta has no patience with clocks. You do. Promise me it will always keep going."
I promised. I brought it here that very day. It worked perfectly. It struck the hours with a beautiful, deep sound. But three weeks later, on a February night, it stopped. At ten past four.
That night Vasile died. At ten past four. I didn't know until the morning, when Elisabeta called me.

She doesn't know. I didn't tell her. For ten years I've been trying to repair it. I changed the spring, cleaned the mechanism, put in new parts. Nothing. Technically, everything is fine. But the clock doesn't want to go.
Maybe it is waiting for something.

When you tell a story, make a small pause before the important event: "Era în spital… și într-o zi… mi-a spus…". The intonation falls at the end of each sentence.
"de-o-da-tă": four syllables, stress on "da". It is said a little louder, for effect.
The pronoun "o" joins the verb: "o-ntorcea" (in fast speech the "î" almost disappears).
In a story the two tenses work together. The imperfect describes the setting and the situation, while the compound perfect says what happened.
descriptions: what it was like, what the weather was like
Ask yourself: "Is it background or an event?" If you can say "and then…?", it is an event → compound perfect.
A very common structure: a long action (imperfect) is interrupted by a short action (compound perfect).
I was reading when the phone rang.
While I was visiting him, he told me a secret.
I was walking down the street and saw Ana.
I was sleeping when Mițu came into the room.
Two long, simultaneous actions both go in the imperfect, linked with "în timp ce":
While I was cooking, he was reading the newspaper.
Grandma used to sing while she made bread.
Then he gave the clock to Grigore.
In the end, Grigore understood why.
Some verbs change their meaning slightly depending on the tense:
știam = I knew the information (for a long time)
am știut = I understood, I found out (at that moment)
l-am cunoscut = I met him for the first time
5. How to tell an oral story
Romanians love telling stories, with lots of details. A few expressions help you sound natural:
And guess what? (expression of surprise: and imagine…)
The listener often reacts with "Nu zău!" (Really?), "Ei, na!", "Și? Și?" or "Ce spui!". Use them to show you are listening.

Ten years ago, Vasile fell ill.
While I was cooking, he was reading.

Maybe the clock is waiting for something.
Do you remember the white rose? The one that appeared next to the photos, on the living-room table? I have solved the mystery. A good tomcat is also a good detective.
It was Tuesday night. The whole house was asleep. I was sitting in my green armchair thinking about life, that is, sleeping with one eye open. Suddenly, I heard a small noise: a door opening slowly.
Nora came out of her room in pyjamas and thick socks. She was holding the white rose, the one from Radu. She tiptoed into the living room so as not to wake Mrs Pop.

The photos were still on the table, side by side. Nora looked at them for a long time. The moonlight came in through the window and lit the faces of the two young men on the rock: Vasile, fifty years ago, and Radu, a week ago.

Then Nora took a small vase from the cabinet, put water in it and placed the rose next to the photos. She whispered something in Swedish. I didn't understand the words, but I understood the tone. It was the tone Mrs Pop uses when she talks to Vasile in front of his photo.
Then she went back to her room. I stayed in the armchair, with both eyes open this time.

In the morning, Mrs Pop found the rose. I was next to her in the kitchen, waiting for breakfast. She stood in front of the vase for a long time. She didn't ask anything. Not at breakfast, not at lunch, not in the evening.
But on Friday evening, when Nora came home from "Ceasul", her eyes were red. Mrs Pop asked her what had happened. Nora only said: "Mr Grigore told me about the clock."
Mrs Pop put the kettle on. Then she said quietly, without turning round: "I know about the clock. I even know what time it stopped. Grigore thinks I don't know."

"I went to the café the day after the funeral. I saw the hands stopped at ten past four. And I saw Grigore's face. I didn't say anything to him. Some people need to carry a secret alone. It's their way of loving."
Then Mrs Pop turned round and smiled. "Thank you for the rose, my dear. Vasile loved white roses."
Nora blushed. "How did you know that I…?"
"That morning Mițu slept on your woollen socks. They were on the living-room rug. This tomcat keeps no secrets."

In the evening, Nora and Mrs Pop drank tea together in the living room, next to the rose. They talked about Vasile, about Radu and about the clock that is silent. Outside it was raining softly. I was sleeping on Mrs Pop's knees and listening. When people talk about important things, their voices become warmer, like a blanket.
It's true. I don't keep secrets. But I have an excuse: those socks were very soft.

Once upon a time, long ago, there was a saint named Ladislaus. He was a king and had a small army.
One day, some enemies were chasing him through the mountains near Turda. Their horses were fast, and his were tired.
The king reached a big rock. He had nowhere left to run.
Then he knelt down and prayed. Suddenly, a loud thunder was heard.
The mountain split in two, and between the rocks a deep chasm appeared.
The enemies could no longer cross. The king was saved.
That is how, the legend says, Turda Gorge came to be. The people of the village still show the marks of the horse's hooves on a stone today.
the legend (old story, not necessarily true)
